title: Is a higher orbit a faster one?
hook: It takes a big rocket burn to lift a satellite to a high orbit. Does it then go faster?

knows: rockets must burn fuel to climb higher
doesNotKnow: that the speed of a circular orbit is set by gravity at that radius, v = sqrt(GM / r)
that gravity weakens with distance from Earth

misconception: A higher orbit is a faster orbit, because it took more energy to get there.
objective: The learner can explain that gravity is weaker farther out, so a circular orbit there needs less speed to keep bending round, and higher orbits are slower and take longer per lap.

claims.text: A circular orbit's speed is set by the radius: v = sqrt(GM / r), with GM for Earth = 3.986 × 10^14 m^3/s^2 and r measured from Earth's centre.
claims.source: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, section 13.4 Satellite Orbits and Energy (v_orbit = sqrt(G M_E / r)). GM_E = 3.986004418e14 m^3/s^2 (IERS Conventions 2010, Table 1.1).

claims.text: At the ISS's orbit radius (6,771 km) the speed is 7.67 km/s and one lap takes 92 minutes; at geostationary radius (42,164 km) it is 3.07 km/s and 23.9 hours.
claims.source: sqrt(3.986e14 / 6.771e6) = 7672 m/s, T = 2 pi r / v = 5545 s = 92.4 min; sqrt(3.986e14 / 4.2164e7) = 3075 m/s, T = 86,166 s = 23.93 h (node; same orbit() as Demo.tsx). Geostationary radius 42,164 km and period one sidereal day 23.93 h: standard values (e.g. NASA/ESA). ISS radius: Earth radius 6371 km + about 400 km altitude, illustrative (the ISS altitude varies, roughly 370-460 km).

claims.text: At 200 km up (radius 6,571 km) the speed is 7.79 km/s and a lap takes 88 minutes; at 20,000 km radius, 4.46 km/s and 7.8 hours.
Earth's gravity falls with the square of the distance from its centre, so at geostationary radius it is about 2.6% as strong as at the ISS.
claims.source: Newton's law of gravitation, g = GM / r^2: (6771 / 42164)^2 = 0.0258.

claims.text: Reaching a higher orbit still takes energy: the satellite gains more height (gravitational) energy than it loses in speed.
claims.source: Circular orbit total energy E = -GMm / (2r), kinetic energy GMm / (2r), potential -GMm / r: raising r raises E though kinetic energy falls. OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, section 13.4.

claims.text: Idealisations: circular orbits around a point-mass Earth, no air drag; the stage is drawn to scale and runs 2,000 times faster than real time.
claims.source: Stated on stage. Drawing: radii in km x 88 / 42164 px; laps take T / 2000 seconds on screen.

recall.question: Two satellites circle the Earth, one 500 km up and one 2,000 km up. Which is moving faster?
recall.why: Gravity is stronger closer in, so a lower circular orbit needs more speed to keep bending round; higher orbits are slower.
